Ok, I think what you're asking is how to set up a network with 
edges and isolates, using an edgelist representation of your data.

There are a couple of ways to do this:

1. You can first create an empty network of the appropriate size using 
network.initialize, and then add the edges from the edgelist using e.g. 
add.edges or network.edgelist.

2. You can add size information to the edgelist by setting the "n" 
attribute (e.g., attr(myedgelist,"n")<-numberofnodes) and then passing it 
to network or as.network.?The size information will be incorporated 
automagically.?(See also ?as.edgelist.sna.)

(all thx go to Carter for this :)

hth,
mm

Hi, Lin and Steve,

Somewhat belatedly, adjusting the density alone will not help with triadic effects. What might help (although only very approximately) is a triadic offset of the form

offset(edges)+offset(gwesp(0, fixed=TRUE))

with

offset.coef=c(-1,+1/3) * (log(Nsim)-log(Nfit))

where Nsim is the network size you are simulating and Nfit is the network size you estimated from.

More details can be found in
Krivitsky, P. N. & Kolaczyk, E. D. (2015) On the Question of Effective Sample Size in Network Modeling: An Asymptotic Inquiry. Statistical Science, 30(2): 184-198.
I hope this helps,
Pavel
On Thu, 2017-12-07 at 08:29 -0800, Steven M Goodreau wrote:

Hi Lin,

When changing the network size, the key is to update the edges coefficient in your model.  The basic idea is to take the edges coefficient and add the natural log of the old network size and then subtract the natural log of the new network size. Equivalently, one can think about partitioning the edges coefficient into two parts: one an offset based on the network size and another the remainder, and then update the offset. Without this update, ergms will preserve density as one changes network size, but with this update, they preserve mean degree. Although the former may seem reasonable on first pass, for most social phenomena the latter makes muc more sense and matches observed behavior much more closely. Note that you do *not* have to update any other coefficients besides the edges.

All this is explained in:

Pavel N. Krivitsky, Mark S. Handcock, and Martina Morris (2011). Adjusting for Network Size and Composition Effects in Exponential-Family Random Graph Models. Statistical Methodology, 8(4): 319?339.

and is also talked about in our Network Modeling for Epidemics course: http://statnet.github.io/nme/

Note, however, that Kirivitsky, Handcock and Morris have - in the paper below, and in subsequent explorations - proven that this works perfectly for dyadic independent terms, and behaves reasonably for some common dyadic dependent terms, but haven't proven it works exactly for the latter. (Co-authors - correct me if I'm wrong on that!!!)

It's not actually 100% clear (at least to me) what the expected behavior should be for something like GWESP when networks change in size - how do we believe explicit triangle closure behaves as networks scale in size, such that the background probably of a triangle being closed declines for the same density? Will the magnitude of the force stay the same, or will people exert more effort to close trinagle in order to get back to the same prportion of their triangles being closed as in a smaller network?  It's tricky stuff, but very intersting, for someone who wanted to explore it in depth with comparative empirical data, like Add Health.

Nevertheless, I believe this simple method should get you close to where you want to be.

Here is some basic example code using a network of size 100 with mean degree of 1, then simulating a network of size 1000 that also has a mean degree of 1, by updating the coefficient form the first model. You should be able to use this as a base, and add in you GWESP and other terms.

library(statnet)
smallnet <- network.initialize(100, directed=F)
smallnet <- san(smallnet~edges, target.stats = 50) # mean deg = 1
smallergm <- ergm(smallnet~edges)

largenet <- network.initialize(1000, directed=F)
largecoef <- smallergm$coef[1] + log(100) - log(1000)
largenet <- simulate(largenet~edges, coef=largecoef)


Cheers,

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Dear Juan,

I would estimate an ERGM on the network that you have observed with
parameters for all the statistics of interest (excluding edges) and then
use those parameters in your simulate() function.
If the goal is to simulate 100 networks, then I would simulate a lot of
networks, say 2000, and from these select those networks that are closest
to the target statistics.
E.g. by calculating all statistics for each network and then calculate the
distance between the statistic vectors of the simulated networks and the
observed statistics. Further, I would exclude deviations you consider too
far.
Another option is to go through every statistic and except say a 2.5%
deviation and exclude all networks that do not meet this criterion for all
statistics.
If 2000 is not enough to get you 100 networks that you like, you can just
add more by simulating with another random number seed. Be careful when
simulating a lot of networks as they tend to be rather big when saved as
network objects in R and several thousand might exceed the RAM of your
machine.

Lastly, if you estimate your ERGM with an edges parameter your other
parameters are estimated conditional on this parameter. Thus, the other
parameters correspond to different statistics, if you exclude the parameter
or fix its statistic to a certain value. This holds of course for every
paramter, but I think the edges parameter, as a sort of intercept, is most
influential here. So, if you use the parameter estimated in mod.e to
simulate, your statistics will not be met. You should condition the
estimation of mod.e also on the number of edges, as you do the
simulation: constraints
= ~edges. That is why I said "excluding edges" above.

The ERGM experts might have a more efficient way how to do it, but this
should work.

Best Regards,

Robert Krause
